title: Assuming FIFO Over Independent HTTP/RPC Request Boundaries
pattern: Invoking multiple asynchronous network requests or RPCs sequentially that modify the same remote entity state, without embedding monotonically increasing sequence numbers or causal dependency markers inside the request payloads.
why_bad: Unreliable networks delay, reorder, or lose packets arbitrarily [20, 21]. Even if requests are sent in order, a network hiccup or parallel server-side processing can cause a later request to arrive first [20, 203]. Without sequence identifiers, the receiver cannot reconstruct the original emission order, leading to permanent state corruption (e.g., a user remaining `Active` instead of `Suspended`) [34, 127].
detection: Identify sequential invocations of asynchronous remote writes/updates against the same logical target in the same code path, where the payloads do not contain structural ordering invariants (e.g., sequence counters, logical clock versions, or causal markers).
fix: Always include a monotonically increasing sequence identifier, transaction ID, or version vector in every state-modifying payload so the recipient can detect and discard out-of-order stale requests [34, 127, 209].
source: Alex Petrov, *Database Internals*, Chapter 8 / passages [20, 34]; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 11 / passages [202, 203, 204].
